debate_title: Compute governance as a lever for AI safety: export contr...

conflicts.point: Whether physical infrastructure telemetry and cryptographic hardware attestation can effectively govern frontier AI labs without disproportionately harming open-source developers and independent labs.

positions.stance: Physical telemetry and automated cryptographic tokens can enforce safety limits on high-density infrastructure while targeted exemptions protect smaller developers from compliance overhead.
Compliance verification processes impose fixed administrative costs and multi-month delays that function as a regressive tax, cementing market oligopolies regardless of statutory exemptions.

conflicts.point: Whether algorithmic efficiency gains and decentralized edge training render hardware-level compute thresholds and static export controls technologically obsolete.

positions.stance: Software optimizations and decentralized training arrays allow models to scale intelligence independently of raw physical cluster density, making hardware thresholds obsolete.
Underlying thermodynamic realities of multi-megawatt training runs remain physically bound to massive power footprints that cannot be concealed by software compression.

verdicts.conflict: Whether physical infrastructure telemetry and cryptographic hardware attestation can effectively govern frontier AI labs without disproportionately harming open-source developers and independent labs.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic position prevails because it accounts for administrative friction and fixed compliance costs that disproportionately burden small developers. The safetyist claim relies on cryptographic hardware attestation tokens—secure data units generated by silicon chips to verify operational limits—but ignores the multi-month administrative review delays identified by the accelerationist camp.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical proof that automated cryptographic attestation completely eliminates human administrative review delays for small-scale developers would reverse this verdict.

verdicts.conflict: Whether algorithmic efficiency gains and decentralized edge training render hardware-level compute thresholds and static export controls technologically obsolete.
verdicts.rationale: The accelerationist argument is stronger because it correctly identifies the limitation of hardware provenance tracking when applied to distributed sub-threshold training runs. While cryptographic hardware attestation verifies silicon provenance, it cannot monitor distributed model training driven by software efficiency gains across multiple smaller clusters.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Demonstrable evidence that the thermodynamic power footprints of multi-megawatt training runs make distributed sub-threshold training economically or physically infeasible would tip the balance.
